action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 76% predicted (35 mL/kg), MIP -58 and MEP 64 cmH2O, weak cough: mildly reduced, FVC above 20 mL/kg
action_criteria.label: Measure respiratory function now (FVC, MIP, MEP, cough)
action_criteria.rationale: Severe bulbar weakness needing a nasogastric tube in a 75-year-old: respiratory muscle strength must be measured at once and trended against the ABN escalation criteria (ICU or HDU if FVC falls below 20 mL/kg or by more than 30%), because bulbar MG can progress to crisis (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: AChR binding and modulating antibodies negative; TSH and free T4 normal
action_criteria.label: Order AChR binding antibody and thyroid function
action_criteria.rationale: Relapsing bulbar weakness with ophthalmoparesis raises a disorder of neuromuscular transmission; AChR binding antibody is the first-line test and TSH screens for thyroid disease (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Decrement of 22% in nasalis and 18% in orbicularis oculi, 6% in ADM; normal CMAPs, no facilitation
action_criteria.label: Order repetitive nerve stimulation including facial muscles
action_criteria.rationale: In bulbar-predominant MG, and in MuSK MG, the decrement is often confined to facial muscles, so nasalis and orbicularis oculi must be tested as well as a limb muscle. Once MuSK antibodies are positive the diagnosis is serological, so RNS is good practice rather than a prerequisite; neurophysiology is mandatory when antibodies are negative (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).

action_criteria.label: Order MuSK antibody after a negative AChR result
action_criteria.rationale: MuSK antibody testing is indicated in every AChR-negative patient; bulbar, facial and neck-predominant weakness is the typical MuSK phenotype (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025; Evoli A et al., Neurol Sci 2019).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal jitter in extensor digitorum communis; increased jitter with 10% blocking in orbicularis oculi
action_criteria.label: Single-fiber EMG including a facial muscle
action_criteria.rationale: Single-fiber EMG of a facial muscle confirms the transmission defect where a limb study may be normal, as in MuSK MG (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No anterior mediastinal mass; age-appropriate thymic involution; no lung mass
action_criteria.label: Order mediastinal CT with contrast
action_criteria.rationale: Thymic imaging is indicated in every patient with MG; thymoma is rare in MuSK MG, but the CT is obtained before the antibody result is known (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No brainstem lesion; no midbrain atrophy; reduced nigral SWI signal
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI for a brainstem lesion and for the parkinsonian syndrome
action_criteria.rationale: Downgaze restriction, axial rigidity, freezing and frontal release signs raise a brainstem lesion and a coexisting atypical parkinsonism; MRI excludes a brainstem lesion and shows no midbrain atrophy, which is what the differential rests on, although a normal midbrain-to-pons proportion does not exclude PSP.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sinus rhythm at 68/min, PR 184 ms, QRS 96 ms, borderline QTc 448 ms; no conduction block.
action_criteria.label: Baseline 12-lead ECG before starting pyridostigmine
action_criteria.rationale: Pyridostigmine can cause bradycardia and atrioventricular block; ABN 2025 advises a baseline ECG before it is started (Jacob 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No interactions with the current medicines
action_criteria.label: Check his medicines against pyridostigmine
action_criteria.rationale: Levodopa-carbidopa and amlodipine have no MG-relevant interaction; optional.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start corticosteroids as an outpatient while bulbar weakness is significant; start them in hospital with bulbar and respiratory monitoring (Evoli 2019).

Avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium unless no alternative exists and the patient is monitored; use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers only at reduced dose with quantitative monitoring.
Do not refer for thymectomy: it is not recommended in MuSK antibody-positive MG (ICG 2020), and the CT shows no thymoma.
Do not attribute the dysphagia and ophthalmoparesis to Parkinson disease or progressive supranuclear palsy before MuSK antibody testing (and neurophysiology when serology is negative).
required_recommendations: Diagnose MuSK antibody-positive myasthenia gravis with severe bulbar and oculomotor involvement (MGFA class IVb, feeding tube without intubation): relapsing fatigable dysphagia and dysarthria, ophthalmoparesis without ptosis, AChR negative, MuSK 42 nmol/L, facial decrement on RNS.

Treat the severe bulbar weakness with plasma exchange (5 exchanges over about 10 days), the preferred acute therapy in MuSK MG (Sanders 2016); if plasma exchange is not available, give IVIG 1 g/kg over 2-3 days for significant bulbar weakness without ventilatory failure (about 65 g at an ideal body weight of 64 kg), or 2 g/kg over 2-5 days (about 130 g) if crisis threatens, after hepatitis B and C serology and an IgG level (Jacob 2025).

Start prednisone in hospital, because bulbar weakness makes steroid-induced worsening dangerous (Evoli 2019): 5-10 mg daily increased by 5 mg on alternate days (after plasma exchange or IVIG: from 10 mg by 5-10 mg every second day) to 30 mg daily, with bulbar and respiratory monitoring (Jacob 2025). Consider rituximab early (1000 mg on days 1 and 14) if the response to initial immunotherapy is unsatisfactory, an early option in MuSK MG (ICG 2020; Jacob 2025; Fionda 2026); an FcRn antagonist (rozanolixizumab is licensed for MuSK antibody-positive generalized MG) is a further escalation option (Fionda 2026).

Before long-term immunosuppression, without delaying urgent treatment: HbA1c, lipids, blood pressure and weight before steroids; before rituximab, hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc), hepatitis C, HIV and varicella zoster serology, TB screening (IGRA), a CD19 count and serum immunoglobulins, with lamivudine prophylaxis if HBsAg or anti-HBc is positive; vaccinations updated at least four weeks before (Jacob 2025; Fionda 2026). During steroids: periodic blood pressure, glucose, weight and eye checks, calcium and vitamin D, and bone densitometry (Fionda 2026).

Use pyridostigmine only cautiously at low dose, if at all, after a baseline ECG: MuSK MG often responds poorly and patients may show cholinergic hypersensitivity, and increased secretions worsen dysphagia (Sanders 2016; Jacob 2025).
Continue nasogastric feeding with aspiration precautions and a speech and language therapy swallowing assessment before oral intake resumes.

Repeat FVC (with MIP and MEP) at least daily while bulbar weakness is severe; refer to ICU or HDU if FVC falls below 20 mL/kg or by more than 30%, or if he cannot complete a sentence, uses accessory muscles or cannot clear secretions (Jacob 2025).

Continue levodopa via the nasogastric tube without interruption during the acute phase, and reassess the parkinsonism (levodopa response, possible coexisting atypical parkinsonism) once the bulbar disease is treated; assess the isolated left upper limb areflexia separately, since MG does not explain it.
Record the MGFA class (here IVb) and a baseline MG-ADL, with QMG where available, to follow treatment against the goal of MG-ADL 0-1 (Fionda 2026; Jacob 2025).

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no role in a disorder of the neuromuscular junction (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).
No cardiac question in this patient; echocardiography does not contribute to the diagnosis of MG.
No palpitations, syncope or arrhythmia; cardiac monitoring does not contribute to the diagnosis of MG.
CSF has no role in MG (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025); it does not address the bulbar weakness.

His freezing, festination and en-bloc turning are already documented on examination; a timed gait and balance battery does not address the bulbar weakness that this admission must diagnose and treat (Jacob 2025).

A formal levodopa challenge needs a 12-hour levodopa withdrawal in a man fed by nasogastric tube with severe bulbar weakness, and his modest levodopa response is already known; the parkinsonism is reassessed once the bulbar disease is treated, not during this admission (Jacob 2025).

His severe hypernasal, hypophonic dysarthria and its fatigability are documented on examination and nothing suggests a language disorder; the speech and language battery tests motor speech and language and never assesses swallowing, which needs a speech and language therapy swallowing assessment (Jacob 2025).
His mild executive dysfunction is already noted on bedside testing; a formal cognitive screen does not address the bulbar weakness and is limited by his dysarthria (Jacob 2025).

A full neuropsychological battery characterizes the dysexecutive features of the parkinsonian syndrome, which is not the question of this admission; it adds nothing to the diagnosis or treatment of MG (Jacob 2025).

A biceps biopsy during one of his two admissions in the past three months already showed no mitochondrial, inflammatory or necrotizing myopathy; repeating an invasive biopsy answers no new question (Jacob 2025).

Dopamine transporter imaging characterizes the known parkinsonism but cannot separate Parkinson disease from atypical parkinsonism and has no role in the bulbar weakness this admission must diagnose and treat (Jacob 2025).

accepted: MuSK antibody-positive myasthenia gravis, bulbar-predominant, with ophthalmoplegia without ptosis

differential.key_features: Possible and not excluded: the downgaze restriction with relatively preserved upgaze and an astonished expression, frontal release signs, axial rigidity with freezing and en-bloc turning, a modest levodopa response and dysexecutive features fit a PSP-like syndrome, and a normal midbrain-to-pons proportion on MRI does not exclude PSP; the brisk masseter reflex fits this upper motor neuron and frontal picture rather than MG. It does not explain the relapsing, fatigable bulbar weakness, which MuSK antibodies and the facial decrement attribute to MG.

differential.diagnosis: Parkinson disease as the cause of the bulbar dysfunction
differential.key_features: Asymmetric rest tremor with a modest levodopa response may reflect coexisting Parkinson disease, but it does not cause relapsing fatigable bulbar weakness or ophthalmoparesis.

Tongue weakness and a brisk masseter reflex raise it, but there are no fasciculations or wasting, the course relapses and remits over two years, and MuSK antibodies are positive; the brisk masseter reflex fits the parkinsonian syndrome.
AChR binding and modulating antibodies negative; MuSK positive.
Single lactate of 2.5 mmol/L normal on repeat, muscle biopsy without COX or SDH abnormality, relapsing course.
Relapsing-remitting fatigable deficits over two years and no brainstem lesion on MRI.

key_clinical_evidence: Two years of relapsing-remitting severe dysphagia with nasal dysarthria, tongue weakness and ophthalmoparesis without ptosis, now needing a nasogastric tube; speech, tongue and jaw weakness are fatigable on examination.
AChR binding and modulating antibodies negative; anti-MuSK antibody 42 nmol/L.
RNS: decrement of 22% in nasalis and 18% in orbicularis oculi with 6% in ADM; SFEMG normal in extensor digitorum and abnormal in orbicularis oculi, the facial-predominant pattern of MuSK MG.
Respiratory function mildly reduced (FVC 35 mL/kg, MIP -58, MEP 64 cmH2O) with a weak cough: FVC above the ABN ICU threshold of 20 mL/kg, but it needs trending.
Mediastinal CT with contrast is indicated in every patient with MG to detect thymoma. Here it shows no thymoma; thymectomy is not recommended in MuSK MG (ICG 2020).
MuSK MG responds poorly to pyridostigmine and well to plasma exchange (Sanders 2016); rituximab is an early option when the response to initial immunotherapy is unsatisfactory (ICG 2020).

Parkinsonism (rest tremor, axial rigidity, gait freezing, supranuclear-pattern downgaze, frontal release signs) may be a coexisting atypical parkinsonism and does not explain the fatigable bulbar weakness; the isolated left upper limb areflexia is not explained by MG.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Fatigable bulbar weakness, fluctuating ophthalmoplegia, and MuSK antibody positivity are MG; Parkinson can coexist but does not explain the fatigable pattern.
red_herrings.data_point: Asymmetric rest tremor diagnosed as possible Parkinson's disease; reduced nigral signal on SWI
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute bulbar dysphagia to PD progression and miss MuSK MG.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The relapsing fatigable bulbar weakness and ophthalmoparesis are explained by neuromuscular transmission failure (facial decrement on RNS, MuSK antibodies). A coexisting PSP-like parkinsonism remains possible, since a normal midbrain-to-pons proportion does not exclude it, but it does not explain the fatigable bulbar pattern.
red_herrings.data_point: Parkinsonism features (tremor, gait, masked facies) suggesting PSP or MSA
red_herrings.intended_effect: Supranuclear eye movement restriction + axial rigidity + poor levodopa response fits PSP or MSA pattern

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Repeat lactate 0.9 mmol/L and a muscle biopsy without COX or SDH abnormality argue against mitochondrial disease; MuSK antibodies establish the neuromuscular junction disorder.
red_herrings.data_point: Single elevated lactate (2.5 mmol/L) suggesting mitochondrial disease
red_herrings.intended_effect: Episodic bulbar dysfunction + mildly elevated lactate raises MELAS concern

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A negative AChR antibody does not exclude MG; MuSK antibody testing in AChR-negative patients is strongly positive.
red_herrings.data_point: Negative AChR antibody on initial testing
red_herrings.intended_effect: Negative AChR antibody might suggest MG is not the diagnosis

sequence_constraints.reason: MuSK antibody testing follows a negative AChR antibody result (Jacob 2025).
Serology comes first: with positive AChR antibodies SFEMG is rarely needed, while every antibody-negative patient needs neurophysiology, RNS first and SFEMG where expertise is available (Jacob 2025).
RNS is the initial neurophysiological test; SFEMG is considered when RNS is normal and suspicion persists, where expertise is available (Jacob 2025).

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: an elderly man with parkinsonism and downgaze restriction has relapsing severe bulbar weakness; AChR antibodies are negative and the diagnosis rests on MuSK testing and facial neurophysiology, while a coexisting atypical parkinsonism stays possible.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 75-year-old man was admitted to the neurology ward for progressive dysphagia requiring nasogastric tube placement, severe dysarthria with hypophonia and nasal speech, and ophthalmoplegia without ptosis. Over the preceding two years, he had experienced similar relapsing and remitting episodes of severe dysphagia that each resolved spontaneously over days to weeks. In the three months prior to admission, he had been hospitalized twice for severe dysphagia. During those admissions a barium swallow, neck CT and a general autoimmune screen had been normal, and his response to three days of IV methylprednisolone was inconsistent. Serum lactate was 2.5 mmol/L on one occasion and 0.9 mmol/L on repeat; anti-Hu, anti-Yo and anti-Ri antibodies were negative; a biceps muscle biopsy showed type I and II fiber atrophy without COX or SDH abnormalities.

At age 72, he had developed an asymmetric rest tremor predominantly in the left leg, followed by the right leg. Brain MRI at that time was normal, and treatment with levodopa-carbidopa produced only modest benefit. On current examination, he had masked facies with decreased blink rate, an astonished expression, and ophthalmoplegia with partial restriction of downward gaze while upward gaze was partially preserved. He had no diplopia. Bulbar examination revealed severe pharyngeal weakness with dysphagia, hypophonia, nasal speech, and marked tongue weakness. Speech became more nasal and less intelligible on sustained counting, and tongue and jaw strength declined with repeated testing. The pharyngeal reflex was normal; masseter reflex was brisk. Frontal release signs (glabellar tap, palmomental, and orbicularis oris reflexes) were present. An asymmetric rest tremor of both legs, worse on the left, was noted. Limb strength was otherwise 5/5 except for areflexia in the left upper limb (with flexor plantar responses bilaterally). Axial rigidity was present with en-bloc turning and gait freezing.
